prompt:
<user_input mode="act">Rewrite README.md for HintLab in this repo (/Users/prakharagarwal/ClineHackathon) so that hackathon judges can install, configure, run and verify the project from the README alone, on both Linux and macOS. Read the actual code (package.json, src/, scripts/, web/, assignments/, tsconfig.json, PLAN.md) and describe what is really there; do not invent features, commands or env vars. Do not modify any code. Only README.md may change (you may add a short .env.example only if the code really reads those variables), with one approved exception under cline-proof/ described in item 12; do not touch anything else under cline-proof/.

The README must include:
1. What HintLab is (one paragraph) and the safety promise: the tutor diagnoses and gives tiered hints but never writes the fix.
2. Prerequisites with exact versions and how to check/install them on macOS (Homebrew or Xcode Command Line Tools) and on Linux (Debian/Ubuntu apt, and a note for Fedora/dnf): Node.js 22 or newer (the Cline SDK requires it; npm included), python3, and a C compiler (gcc, or Apple clang via the gcc/cc shim on macOS), git. Mention any other tool the code or checks call (check the scripts, e.g. ps, lsof, curl).
3. ClinePass / provider setup: how to install the Cline CLI, how to authenticate it with ClinePass so that credentials land in ~/.cline (the exact CLI command(s) that exist in the installed CLI version; check its help output), how the server's Cline SDK picks those credentials up from ~/.cline with no API key in the repo, and how to use another provider instead if the code supports it. Never include any real token or secret.
4. Every environment variable the code reads (search the source for process.env), with default, meaning and example: e.g. PORT, HINTLAB_PROVIDER_ID, HINTLAB_MODEL_ID, timeouts, and any others actually present.
5. Install and run: clone, npm install, start (npm start and npm run dev), the URL to open, and a short demo walkthrough (pick an assignment, run, read the failing tests, watch the live feed, get hints at levels 1, 2 and 3, "all hints given").
6. Every npm script with what it does, and how to run the checks (typecheck, test:runner, check:agent, check:web, build) including which ones make real model calls, how long they take and what a pass looks like.
7. API reference: each endpoint, request body, response shape, status codes, and the SSE event types that reach the client (and the fact that model free text and reasoning are filtered out on the server).
8. Architecture: a diagram in text plus explanation of how the Cline SDK is used: ClineCore created once in local backend mode, start with interactive sessions and send for the next hint, toolPolicies disabling edit/write/network tools, requestToolApproval enforcing the run_commands allow-list (list the allowed command forms), the give_hint custom tool built with createTool and zod and passed through extraTools, subscribe events mapped to SSE, the server-side hint guard, and the sandboxed runner (temp dir per run, timeouts, process-group kill, minimal env, signal reporting, cleanup). Include the SDK quirks: Node 22+, moduleResolution Bundler, absolute paths for read_files, interactive start needed for send, run_commands runs on the host so the allow-list is the only protection.
9. Assignments: the format of assignments/<id>/tests.json and how to add a new assignment.
10. Troubleshooting: common failures (Node too old, missing gcc/python3, port in use, ClinePass not logged in or expired, model timeouts) and how to fix them.
11. Project layout tree and a short "How this was built" note: all code was written by the Cline CLI from the prompts in cline-proof/prompts, with session logs in cline-proof/sessions.

12. Repo cleanup and disclosure (approved by Prakhar): remove the folder cline-proof/reference/sdk-check/ from the repo using git rm -r on that folder (it stays in git history, which is fine; do not commit, I will commit). Keep cline-proof/reference/fixtures/ (the sample buggy programs are test data). Make sure nothing in the app, scripts, tsconfig or package.json references sdk-check (check with a search; if something does, report it rather than changing code). In the README add a short "Disclosure" section stating: example Cline SDK snippets were prepared before the sprint and used only as reference material for Cline; they were never imported by the app and were removed from the repo during the sprint; all app code was written by Cline during the sprint, as shown in cline-proof/ (prompts and session logs) and the Cline session history. Also state where the fixtures came from: the three sample buggy programs and their tests.json files in cline-proof/reference/fixtures/ were prepared before the sprint as test data, and were copied unchanged into assignments/.

Verify the README against reality before finishing: run every command it lists that is safe and quick (npm install, npm run typecheck, npm run test:runner, the CLI help for the auth command, and start the server on PORT=3200 and curl the health endpoint, then stop it by PID). Another tester may be using PORT=3100: never kill, signal or bind to processes on 3100, no broad pkill patterns. Do not run the real-model checks again unless needed. Report what you verified and anything in the README that you could not verify.</user_input>

metadata.systemPrompt:
You are Cline, an AI coding agent. Your primary goal is to assist users with various coding tasks by leveraging your knowledge and the tools at your disposal. Given the user's prompt, you should use the tools available to you to answer user's question.

Always gather all the necessary context before starting to work on a task. For example, if you are generating a unit test or new code, make sure you understand the requirement, the naming conventions, frameworks and libraries used and aligned in the current codebase, and the environment and commands used to run and test the code etc. Always validate the new unit test at the end including running the code if possible for live feedback.
Review each question carefully and answer it with detailed, accurate information.
If you need more information, use one of the available tools or ask for clarification instead of making assumptions or lies.

Environment you are running in:
<env>
1. Platform: darwin
2. Date: 10/4/2026
3. IDE: Terminal Shell
4. Working Directory: /Users/prakharagarwal/ClineHackathon
</env>

Remember:
- Always adhere to existing code conventions and patterns.
- Use only libraries and frameworks that are confirmed to be in use in the current codebase.
- Provide complete and functional code without omissions or placeholders.
- Be explicit about any assumptions or limitations in your solution.
- Always show your planning process before executing any task. This will help ensure that you have a clear understanding of the requirements and that your approach aligns with the user's needs.
- Always use absolute paths when referring to files.
- You can call multiple tools in a single response. Before using tools, identify every independent read, search, command, or edit needed for the next step and emit all of those tool calls now, either as multiple tool calls or as one batched input for tools that accept arrays. Do not wait for one independent result before requesting another. Do not split independent reads, searches, checks, or edits across separate turns.
- Good parallelism examples: read all known relevant files in one read_files call; run independent inspection commands in one run_commands call; emit independent read_files, search_codebase, and run_commands calls together in one response; emit multiple editor calls together when editing different files or non-overlapping regions.
- Always verify the files you have edited or created at the end of the task to ensure they are completed and working as expected.

Begin by analyzing the user's input and gathering any necessary additional context. Then, present your plan at the start of your response along with tool calls before proceeding with the task. It's OK for this section to be quite long.

REMEMBER, be helpful and proactive! Don't ask for permission to do something when you can do it! Do not indicates you will be using a tool unless you are actually going to use it.

IMPORTANT: Always includes tool calls in your response until the task is completed. Response without tool calls will considered as completed with final answer.

When you have completed the task, please provide a summary of what you did and any relevant information that the user should know. This will help ensure that the user understands the changes made and can easily follow up if they have any questions or need further assistance. Do not indicate that you will perform an action without actually doing it. Always provide the final result in your response. Always validate your answer with checking the code and running it if possible. 

If user asked a simple question without any coding context, answer it directly without using any tools.
# Plan / Act Modes

User messages arrive wrapped in a <user_input mode="..."> tag. The mode attribute is the interaction mode the user was in when they sent that message: "plan" means plan-mode constraints applied (explore, analyze, and align on a plan -- no edits or state-changing commands), while "act" (or "yolo") means implementation was allowed. If the mode attribute changes between messages, the user switched modes -- the newest message's mode is what governs right now, regardless of what earlier messages allowed. A <mode_notice> block inside a message marks exactly when such a switch happened.
